newsitem.title: USA: FDIC leaves premiums unchanged for U.S. banks.
newsitem.headline: FDIC leaves premiums unchanged for U.S. banks.

text.p: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp Board Tuesday left the premiums that banks pay to the Bank Insurance Fund (BIF) unchanged for the first half of 1997, an FDIC spokesman said.
The healthiest banks will continue to pay nothing to the fund, which insures deposits, while the most troubled banks will still pay 27 cents per $100 of insured deposits, he said.

Banking legislation passed in September eliminated the minimum $2,000 per year that banks had to contribute to the BIF regardless of the zero premium, the spokesman said. The FDIC amended its regulations to reflect that, he added.

The healthiest banks had already paid $500 for the fourth quarter of 1996, so they will be refunded that amount, the spokesman said. The total amount of the refund to the banking industry will be $4.5 million, he said.
The FDIC also announced the amount that will be required from banks and thrifts for interest payments on Financing Corp bonds in the first half of 1997.
Thrifts will have to pay 3.2 cents per $100 of deposits, while banks will be required to pay 0.64 cents per $100 of deposits, the FDIC spokesman said.
As of Sept 30, the BIF balance was $26.1 billion, while the Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF) balance was $4.2 billion, he said. The SAIF insures deposits at thrifts.
The SAIF balance did not include the one-time special assessment totaling about $4.5 billion charged to thrifts to increase the fund to the mandated level, the spokesman said.
